title: Sampling & Discrete Time
description: Sample signals without aliasing, describe sequences with the z-transform and read spectra from DFT bins.

study.title: The sampling theorem
study.body: Sampling $x(t)$ every $T_s$ seconds ($f_s = 1/T_s$) makes the spectrum periodic: copies of $X(f)$ appear around every multiple of $f_s$. If $x(t)$ is band-limited to $B$ and $f_s > 2B$, the copies do not overlap and $x(t)$ can be recovered exactly from its samples. $2B$ is the **Nyquist rate**; $f_s/2$ is the Nyquist (folding) frequency.

study.title: Aliasing
study.body: If $f_s < 2B$, the copies overlap and high frequencies masquerade as low ones. A sinusoid at $f_0$ produces exactly the same samples as one at $|f_0 - kf_s|$ for any integer $k$; after reconstruction it appears at the alias in $0 \ldots f_s/2$, using the multiple $kf_s$ nearest to $f_0$. Drag $f_0$: below $f_s/2$ the red reconstruction lies on the grey signal; above it the same dots trace a slower red wave, which folds back to 0 at $f_0 = f_s$.

study.title: Reconstruction and anti-aliasing
study.body: An ideal low-pass filter with cutoff $f_s/2$ keeps only the original copy of the spectrum; in time this is sinc interpolation between the samples. In practice an **anti-aliasing** low-pass filter removes everything above $f_s/2$ **before** the sampler, and the DAC output is smoothed by a reconstruction filter. Sampling well above $2B$ (oversampling) leaves room for gentle filters.

study.title: Discrete-time signals
study.body: The samples form a sequence $x[n] = x(nT_s)$. A sinusoid $\cos(2\pi f_0 t)$ becomes $\cos(\Omega n)$ with the discrete frequency $\Omega$ in rad/sample. $\Omega$ and $\Omega + 2\pi$ give identical sequences, so only $0 \leq \Omega \leq \pi$ (i.e. $0 \ldots f_s/2$) is unique: aliasing again. Basic sequences: $\delta[n]$, $u[n]$, $a^n u[n]$.

study.title: The z-transform
study.body: The discrete counterpart of the Laplace transform. Pairs: $\delta[n] \to 1$, $u[n] \to \frac{z}{z - 1}$, $a^n u[n] \to \frac{z}{z - a}$ for $|z| > |a|$. A delay of one sample multiplies by $z^{-1}$. A causal system $H(z)$ is stable when all its poles lie **inside the unit circle** $|z| < 1$; $a^n$ decays only if $|a| < 1$.

study.title: The DFT and frequency resolution
study.body: The DFT turns $N$ samples into $N$ frequency bins $X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]e^{-j2\pi kn/N}$. Bin $k$ corresponds to $f_k = k f_s/N$ (for $k \leq N/2$). The bin spacing, the **frequency resolution**, is $f_s/N$ = 1 / (record length). Zero-padding interpolates the spectrum but does not improve the true resolution; only a longer record does.

steps.title: Sampling
steps.body: An ADC measures $x(t)$ every $T_s$ seconds. The **sampling theorem**: a signal with no frequencies above $B$ is completely determined by its samples if the sampling rate exceeds twice the bandwidth. The minimum rate $2B$ is the **Nyquist rate**.

steps.prompt: An audio signal contains frequencies up to {{B|Hz}}. What is its Nyquist rate?
steps.explanation: The Nyquist rate is twice the highest frequency: $2B$ = 2 × {{B|Hz}} = {{2*B|Hz}}. Sampling must be faster than this to avoid aliasing.

steps.prompt: What is the minimum sampling rate for $x(t) = \cos(2\pi \cdot {{f1}}t) + 3\sin(2\pi \cdot {{f2}}t)$ (frequencies in Hz)?
steps.explanation: The highest frequency present is {{f2|Hz}} (the amplitude 3 does not matter). The Nyquist rate is $2f_{max}$ = {{2*f2|Hz}}. Adding the frequencies is wrong: a **sum** of sinusoids contains only the original frequencies.

steps.title: Aliasing
steps.body: Sample too slowly and a high frequency produces the **same samples** as a lower one. The graph shows a sine at $0.9f_s$ (grey) and one at $0.1f_s$ (red): they pass through identical sample points. After reconstruction you hear the $0.1f_s$ tone, the **alias**. In general $kf_s$ is the multiple of $f_s$ nearest to $f_0$.

steps.prompt: A {{f0|Hz}} sinusoid is sampled at {{fs|Hz}} without an anti-aliasing filter. At what frequency does it appear after reconstruction?
steps.explanation: {{f0|Hz}} is above the Nyquist frequency $f_s/2$ = {{fs/2|Hz}}, so it aliases. The nearest multiple of $f_s$ is $f_s$ itself: $f_a = |f_0 - f_s|$ = |{{f0|Hz}} − {{fs|Hz}}| = {{fs-f0|Hz}}. It folds back around $f_s/2$.

steps.title: Try it: aliasing
steps.body: A cosine at $f_0$ is sampled at $f_s$ = 1 kHz (dots). The red dashed curve is what an ideal reconstruction makes of the samples. Drag $f_0$ past 500 Hz: the apparent frequency falls again, reaching 0 at 1 kHz, and rises once more up to 1.5 kHz. Any $f_0$ and $|f_0 - kf_s|$ give the same dots.

steps.title: Discrete-time frequency
steps.body: The samples form a sequence $x[n] = x(nT_s)$. A sinusoid $\cos(2\pi f_0 t)$ becomes $\cos(\Omega n)$, where the **discrete frequency** $\Omega$ is measured in radians per sample. $\Omega = \pi$ corresponds to $f_s/2$, the highest frequency a sequence can represent.

steps.prompt: A {{f0|Hz}} sinusoid is sampled at {{fs|Hz}}. Find its discrete frequency $\Omega$ in rad/sample.
steps.explanation: $\Omega = 2\pi f_0/f_s$ = 2π × {{f0}}/{{fs}} = {{2*pi*f0/fs}} rad/sample. That is {{f0/fs}} of a full cycle per sample.

steps.title: The z-transform
steps.body: For sequences, the z-transform plays the role of the Laplace transform. Each sample is weighted by a power of $z^{-1}$, so $z^{-1}$ stands for a delay of one sample.

steps.prompt: What is the z-transform of $x[n] = \delta[n - {{k}}]$, a single unit sample at $n$ = {{k}}?
steps.explanation: Only the term $n$ = {{k}} survives in $\sum x[n]z^{-n}$, so $X(z) = z^{-{{k}}}$. A delay of {{k}} samples multiplies the transform by $z^{-{{k}}}$; the undelayed $\delta[n]$ has transform 1.

steps.prompt: A band-limited signal is sampled at $f_s = 2.5B$. Which cutoff is the standard choice for the ideal reconstruction low-pass filter?
steps.explanation: The sampled spectrum contains the original between $-B$ and $B$ plus copies centred on multiples of $f_s$. The filter must keep the original and remove the copies; the cutoff halfway, at $f_s/2 = 1.25B$, has margin on both sides. $B/2$ would cut away part of the signal, $f_s$ and $2f_s$ would let copies through.

steps.title: DFT bins
steps.body: The DFT of $N$ samples gives $N$ bins. Bin $k$ sits at $f_k = kf_s/N$ and the bins are $\Delta f = f_s/N$ apart. Since $N/f_s$ is the record length $T_0$, the resolution is $1/T_0$: to see finer frequency detail you must record longer.

steps.prompt: A {{f0|Hz}} tone is sampled at {{fs|Hz}} with no anti-aliasing filter. Which frequency between 0 and $f_s/2$ appears after reconstruction?
steps.explanation:
Find the multiple of $f_s$ nearest to $f_0$: $f_0/f_s$ = {{f0/fs}}, so $k$ = {{round(f0/fs)}}.
$f_a = |f_0 - kf_s|$ = |{{f0|Hz}} − {{round(f0/fs)}} × {{fs|Hz}}| = {{abs(f0-fs*round(f0/fs))|Hz}}.

steps.prompt: A signal sampled at {{fs|Hz}} is analysed with an $N$ = {{N||4}}-point DFT.

ask.explanation: $N$ samples spaced $T_s = 1/f_s$ apart: $T_0 = N/f_s$ = {{N||4}} / {{fs}} = {{N/fs|s}}. (The resolution is $1/T_0$ = {{fs/N|Hz}}.)

steps.prompt: A {{N||4}}-point DFT is taken of a signal sampled at {{fs|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: A tone at {{fk|Hz|4}} falls exactly on a bin. Which bin index $k$?

steps.prompt: Signals sampled at {{fs|Hz}} must be analysed with a frequency resolution of {{df|Hz}}.

ask.explanation: $\Delta f = f_s/N$, so $N = f_s/\Delta f$ = {{fs}} / {{df}} = {{fs/df||4}} samples.

ask.prompt: How long must the record be?
ask.explanation: The resolution is 1 / (record length), so $T_0 = 1/\Delta f$ = 1 / {{df|Hz}} = {{1/df|s}}, whatever the sampling rate.

steps.prompt: What is the z-transform of the sequence $x[0]$ = {{c0}}, $x[1]$ = {{c1}}, $x[2]$ = {{c2}} (zero elsewhere)?
steps.explanation: $X(z) = \sum x[n]z^{-n}$: sample $n$ gets the factor $z^{-n}$. So $X(z)$ = {{c0}} + {{c1}}$z^{-1}$ + {{c2}}$z^{-2}$. Positive powers of $z$ would mean samples at negative $n$.

steps.prompt: A causal system with impulse response $h[n] = ({{a}})^n u[n]$ is stable.
steps.explanation: $H(z) = \frac{z}{z - a}$ has a pole at $z = a$ = {{a}}. A causal system is stable if all poles lie inside the unit circle, $|a| < 1$, so that $a^n$ dies out. Here $|a|$ = {{abs(a)}}.

steps.prompt: Match each sequence to its z-transform.
steps.explanation: $a^n u[n]$ is a geometric series: $\sum (az^{-1})^n = \frac{1}{1 - az^{-1}} = \frac{z}{z - a}$. With $a = 1$ it gives the step. A one-sample delay multiplies by $z^{-1}$, and the ramp has a double pole at $z = 1$.

steps.prompt: A filter computes $y[n] = {{a}}\,y[n-1] + x[n]$. Find its impulse response $h[n]$ at $n$ = {{k}}.
The graph shows the magnitude spectrum of a band-limited signal.

ask.explanation: The spectrum ends at $B$ = {{B|Hz}}, so the Nyquist rate is $2B$ = {{2*B|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: It is sampled at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}. Above which frequency is the reconstructed signal corrupted by aliasing?
ask.explanation: The spectrum reaches $B$ = {{B|Hz}}. The copy centred on $f_s$ reaches down to $f_s - B$ = {{fs|Hz}} − {{B|Hz}} = {{fs-B|Hz}}. Between there and $f_s/2$ = {{fs/2|Hz}} the copies overlap the original, so everything above {{fs-B|Hz}} is corrupted.

steps.prompt: A signal band-limited to $B$ is sampled at $f_s = 3B$. Which graph shows the spectrum of the sampled signal? (Horizontal axis from $-7B$ to $7B$.)
steps.explanation: Sampling repeats $X(f)$ around every multiple of $f_s = 3B$: copies centred at $0, \pm 3B, \pm 6B, \ldots$ With $f_s > 2B$ they do not overlap (gaps from $B$ to $2B$). Overlapping copies mean $f_s < 2B$ (here $1.5B$); copies that just touch mean $f_s = 2B$; a single copy is the unsampled signal.

steps.prompt: A cosine is sampled at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}} (dots). Find an input frequency **above** $f_s/2$ whose samples lie on the dashed orange {{fa|Hz}} cosine, i.e. that aliases to {{fa|Hz}}.
steps.hint: Aliases of $f_0$ are $|f_0 - kf_s|$. Which $f_0$ above {{fs/2|Hz}} is {{fa|Hz}} away from a multiple of $f_s$?
steps.explanation: A cosine at $f_0$ and one at $|f_0 - kf_s|$ give identical samples, because $\cos(2\pi f_0 nT_s)$ only changes by whole turns $2\pi kn$. So every $f_0 = kf_s \pm f_a$ works: {{fs-fa|Hz}}, {{fs+fa|Hz}}, {{2*fs-fa|Hz}}, {{2*fs+fa|Hz}}, … The grey signal wiggles fast between the dots, but the dots only show the slow {{fa|Hz}} wave. This is why the anti-aliasing filter must remove everything above {{fs/2|Hz}} **before** sampling.

steps.prompt: What is the Nyquist rate of $x(t) = \cos(2\pi \cdot {{f1}}t)\cos(2\pi \cdot {{f2}}t)$ (frequencies in Hz)?
steps.explanation: A product of cosines contains the sum and difference frequencies: $\frac{1}{2}[\cos 2\pi({{f2-f1}})t + \cos 2\pi({{f1+f2}})t]$. The highest is {{f1+f2|Hz}}, so the Nyquist rate is {{2*(f1+f2)|Hz}}. (Taking $2f_2$ = {{2*f2|Hz}} would alias the sum component.)

steps.prompt: The filter $y[n] = {{a}}\,y[n-1] + x[n]$ receives a constant input $x[n]$ = {{X0}} for $n \geq 0$. What value does $y[n]$ settle to?
steps.explanation: $H(z) = \frac{z}{z - {{a}}}$ has its pole inside the unit circle, so the output settles. The DC gain is $H(1) = \frac{1}{1 - {{a}}}$ = {{1/(1-a)}}, so $y \to$ {{X0}} × {{1/(1-a)}} = {{X0/(1-a)}}. (Check: in steady state $y = {{a}}y + {{X0}}$.)

steps.prompt: A {{f0|Hz}} tone is sampled at {{fs|Hz}} and analysed with an $N$ = {{N||4}}-point DFT. Which bin $k$ (between 0 and $N/2$) shows the largest magnitude?
steps.explanation: Bin $k$ is at $kf_s/N$, so the tone sits at $k = f_0N/f_s$ = {{f0}} × {{N||4}} / {{fs}} = {{f0*N/fs||4}}. It falls between bins; the nearest one, $k$ = {{round(f0*N/fs)}}, is the largest. (Some energy leaks into the neighbouring bins.)

steps.prompt: Put the blocks of a digital signal-processing chain in order.
steps.explanation: The anti-aliasing filter must come **before** sampling: once aliased, components cannot be separated from genuine ones. After processing, the DAC holds each value for $T_s$ (a staircase) and the reconstruction filter removes the copies of the spectrum around multiples of $f_s$.

steps.prompt: The anti-aliasing filter can be placed **after** the sampler, as long as it is a good low-pass filter.
steps.explanation: Aliasing happens at the moment of sampling: a 0.9$f_s$ component produces exactly the same samples as a 0.1$f_s$ one. No filter afterwards can tell them apart. The low-pass filter must remove everything above $f_s/2$ before the signal is sampled.

steps.prompt: Zero-padding a record from $N$ to $4N$ samples before the DFT lets you separate two tones that are closer together than $f_s/N$.
steps.explanation: Zero-padding adds no new information: it only computes the same underlying spectrum at more closely spaced points (interpolation). The ability to separate two tones is set by the record length $T_0 = N/f_s$: about $1/T_0 = f_s/N$. To resolve closer tones you need a longer record.
